example.en: I'm just one sticker away from filling the album.

packs.name: Essentials VI
packs.title: Football · Essentials VI
packs.about: The words of the stands and the pitch.

words.note: A casual game among friends, usually fútbol cinco. Also flashy play that gets nowhere.

example.es: Los jueves jugamos al fulbito con los del laburo.
example.en: On Thursdays we play a casual football game with the people from work.

words.note: Elsewhere often autogol. Also used for any self-inflicted mistake.

example.es: Perdimos por un gol en contra en el último minuto.
example.en: We lost because of an own goal in the last minute.

words.note: "¿Por quién hinchás?" asks your team. "No hinches" also means stop bugging me.

example.es: ¿Vos por quién hinchás?
example.en: Which team do you support?

words.note: To go down to the second division. River's 2011 relegation is still the classic joke; also said jokingly of anything going downhill.

example.es: Si perdemos hoy, nos vamos a la B.
example.en: If we lose today, we drop to the second division.

words.note: Table football, a classic in bars and clubs. From "mete gol", score a goal.

example.es: ¿Jugamos un metegol mientras esperamos la pizza?
example.en: Do you want to play table football while we wait for the pizza?

packs.name: Going deeper I
packs.title: Football · Going deeper I
packs.about: The words of the stands and the pitch.

words.note: Named for the white and sky-blue shirt. Common in sports news; fans usually say "la Selección".

example.es: La albiceleste juega el martes en el Monumental.
example.en: The national team plays Tuesday at the Monumental.

words.note: A fake move, in football or in life. The verb is "amagar": to fake.

example.es: Con un amague lo dejó sentado al defensor.
example.en: With one fake move he left the defender on the ground.

words.note: A footballer's wife or girlfriend. From "botines", football boots. Mocking: it suggests she is with him for money and fame. Don't say it to someone.

example.es: Salió en la tele con otra botinera famosa.
example.en: She was on TV with another famous footballer's girlfriend.

words.note: A fan chant sung in the stands, often mocking the rival.

example.es: La hinchada inventó un cantito nuevo para el clásico.
example.en: The fans made up a new song for the big match.

words.note: The classic number 10 who links midfield and attack. Riquelme is the textbook example.

example.es: A este equipo le falta un enganche como Riquelme.
example.en: This team needs a creative player like Riquelme.

packs.name: Going deeper II
packs.title: Football · Going deeper II
packs.about: The words of the stands and the pitch.

words.note: The full calendar of matches in a tournament. From English, pronounced "fíxtur".

example.es: Mirá el fixture, nos toca River en la tercera fecha.
example.en: Look at the schedule, we play River in the third round.

words.note: Juggling the ball without letting it touch the ground. "Hacer jueguito".

example.es: El nene hace cien jueguitos sin que se le caiga.
example.en: The kid kicks the ball up a hundred times without dropping it.

words.note: The cheapest standing section of the stadium, where the loudest fans go.

example.es: Siempre voy a la popular con mi viejo.
example.en: I always go to the cheap standing area with my dad.

words.note: From River's nickname "los Millonarios". Mostly heard in the news; fans usually just say "soy de River", rivals say "gallina".

example.es: Mi viejo es millonario y mi vieja bostera.
example.en: My dad supports River and my mom supports Boca.

words.note: A player who never passes. From "morfar", to eat: he eats the ball.

example.es: Pasala, morfón, que estoy solo.
example.en: Pass it, you selfish player, I'm free.

packs.name: Going deeper III
packs.title: Football · Going deeper III
packs.about: The words of the stands and the pitch.

words.note: Argentine spelling and pronunciation of "offside". Also in daily life: "me agarraste en orsai" = you caught me off guard.

example.es: El gol no vale, estaba en orsai.
example.en: The goal doesn't count, he was offside.

words.note: Someone terrible at football, all kicks and no touch. Teasing among friends.

example.es: No me elijan, soy un patadura.
example.en: Don't pick me, I'm bad at football.

words.note: Usually written as two words, "pecho frío". A player who shows no passion for the shirt; also said of anyone cold. A harsh insult.

example.es: Ese nueve es un pechofrío, no corre nunca.
example.en: That striker has no heart, he never runs.

words.note: The players of a team, used a lot in sports news.

example.es: El plantel entrenó a puertas cerradas.
example.en: The team trained behind closed doors.

words.note: Football: a very hard, powerful shot. Loved by commentators.

example.es: Le pegó de afuera del área, un taponazo al ángulo.
example.en: He hit it from outside the area, a very strong shot into the top corner.

packs.name: Essentials I
packs.title: Politics & society · Essentials I
packs.about: Parties, protests and the country in the news.

words.note: The ring of districts around the capital, where about a quarter of the country lives. Key in every election.

example.es: Nací en el conurbano, en Lomas de Zamora.
example.en: I was born in the suburbs, in Lomas de Zamora.

words.note: A street demonstration. Very common in Buenos Aires, often ending at Plaza de Mayo or Congreso.

example.es: Mañana hay marcha en el centro, mejor andá en subte.
example.en: There's a protest march downtown tomorrow, better take the subway.

words.note: A strike, from one sector to a "paro general". "Hay paro de colectivos": there are no buses today.

example.es: Mañana hay paro de trenes, así que voy en bondi.
example.en: Tomorrow there's a train strike, so I'm taking the bus.

words.note: The movement founded by Juan Perón; still the central divide of Argentine politics.

example.es: En mi familia el peronismo es casi una religión.
example.en: In my family, Peronism is almost a religion.

words.note: When the government cuts spending: lower pensions, fewer subsidies, higher bills. A loaded word in the news and at protests.

example.es: El ajuste lo pagan los jubilados.
example.en: Retired people are paying for the spending cuts.

packs.name: Essentials II
packs.title: Politics & society · Essentials II
packs.about: Parties, protests and the country in the news.

words.note: The usual word for a trade union. "Los gremios" have huge political weight in Argentina.

example.es: El gremio de los docentes convocó a un paro.
example.en: The teachers' union called a strike.

words.note: The deep split between Kirchnerists and anti-Kirchnerists that divides families and friends.

example.es: En mi familia la grieta arruina todos los asados.
example.en: In my family the political divide ruins every barbecue.

words.note: Political movement of Néstor and Cristina Kirchner, part of Peronism.

example.es: El kirchnerismo ganó en la provincia de Buenos Aires.
example.en: Kirchnerism won in Buenos Aires province.

words.note: A supporter of Perón's movement. Also an adjective: "un gobierno peronista".

example.es: Mi abuelo era peronista de toda la vida.
example.en: My grandpa was a lifelong Peronist.

words.note: Protesters block a street or road so traffic cannot pass. A daily reason for being late in Buenos Aires.

example.es: Hay un piquete en la 9 de Julio, llego tarde.
example.en: There's a road block on 9 de Julio, I'll be late.

packs.name: Essentials III
packs.title: Politics & society · Essentials III
packs.about: Parties, protests and the country in the news.

words.note: A protest where people bang pots and pans from balconies or in the street.

example.es: Anoche hubo cacerolazo en todo el barrio.
example.en: Last night there was a pot-banging protest all over the neighborhood.

words.note: Made popular by Javier Milei to attack career politicians.

example.es: Dice que va a terminar con los privilegios de la casta.
example.en: He says he'll end the privileges of the political elite.

words.note: Short for fascista. Used loosely for anyone authoritarian or hard right.

example.es: Ese tipo es re facho, quiere meter presos a todos.
example.en: That guy is really fascist, he wants to put everyone in jail.

words.note: Supporter of Néstor and Cristina Kirchner; short form "K". Opponents say "kuka", an insult from "cucaracha" (cockroach): do not repeat it.

example.es: Toda mi familia es kirchnerista.
example.en: My whole family is pro-Kirchner.

packs.name: Essentials IV
packs.title: Politics & society · Essentials IV
packs.about: Parties, protests and the country in the news.

words.note: In Argentina it means pro free market and small state, not left-leaning like in the US. Milei's followers call themselves "libertarios".

example.es: Mi primo se hizo liberal y ahora habla solo de impuestos.
example.en: My cousin became a free-market supporter and now only talks about taxes.

words.note: Literally left-handed, and neutral in that sense. Politically, a leftist: often a jab, and an insult if said to someone's face.

example.es: Mi tío dice que todos los profesores son zurdos.
example.en: My uncle says all teachers are leftists.

words.note: Political label for someone who hates Peronism, since the 1955 coup.

example.es: Mi abuelo era re gorila, odiaba a Perón.
example.en: My grandfather was a strong anti-Peronist, he hated Perón.

words.note: Someone on the public payroll who only shows up on payday. Gnocchi are traditionally eaten on the 29th, around when salaries are paid.

example.es: Ese es un ñoqui, aparece solo para cobrar.
example.en: That guy's a fake employee, he only shows up to get paid.

words.note: A protester who blocks roads, a symbol of Argentine social movements since the 90s.

example.es: Los piqueteros cortaron la avenida toda la mañana.
example.en: The protesters blocked the avenue all morning.

packs.name: Going deeper I
packs.title: Politics & society · Going deeper I
packs.about: Parties, protests and the country in the news.

words.note: A presidential second round. From French; also written "ballotage" and then pronounced "ba-lo-TASH".

example.es: Si nadie gana en primera vuelta, hay balotaje.
example.en: If nobody wins the first round, there's a second round.

words.note: A presidential speech that all TV and radio stations must air at once.

example.es: Cortaron la novela por una cadena nacional.
example.en: They cut the soap opera for a presidential broadcast.

words.note: To stall a project by leaving it in a drawer. Common about bills in Congress.

example.es: El Congreso cajoneó el proyecto de ley.
example.en: Congress put the new law on hold.

words.note: Member of La Cámpora, the Kirchnerist youth group named after President Héctor Cámpora.

example.es: Mi primo es camporista y milita en el barrio.
example.en: My cousin is in La Cámpora and is a political activist in the neighborhood.

words.note: Government limits on buying dollars; "salir del cepo" means lifting them. Mostly lifted for individuals in April 2025, but the word is still in the news.

example.es: Con el cepo no se podían comprar más de doscientos dólares.
example.en: With the controls, you couldn't buy more than two hundred dollars.

packs.name: Going deeper II
packs.title: Politics & society · Going deeper II
packs.about: Parties, protests and the country in the news.

words.note: The 2001 limit on taking cash out of banks, part of a huge crisis. In daily life it's also a baby's playpen.

example.es: Con el corralito mis viejos perdieron sus ahorros.
example.en: When the banks froze the money, my parents lost their savings.

words.note: Protesters blocking a road or highway, the signature tactic of piqueteros.

example.es: Hay un corte de ruta en la Panamericana, andá por otro lado.
example.en: There's a road block on the highway, go another way.

words.note: A follower of ex-president Cristina Kirchner. Also an adjective.

example.es: Mi tío es re cristinista, no le hables de política.
example.en: My uncle is a big Cristina supporter, don't talk to him about politics.

words.note: To publicly expose someone, online or with a protest outside their home. Also "escracharse": to crash hard.

example.es: Lo escracharon en las redes por lo que dijo.
example.en: He was publicly shamed on social media for what he said.

words.note: The official name of the Peronist party is Partido Justicialista, or PJ.

example.es: Es el candidato del Partido Justicialista.
example.en: He's the candidate of the Peronist party.

packs.name: Going deeper III
packs.title: Politics & society · Going deeper III
packs.about: Parties, protests and the country in the news.

words.note: From K (Kirchner) + "cucaracha", cockroach. Insult used by anti-Kirchner people, common online. Saying it means taking a political side; better not to use it.

example.es: En las redes le dicen kuka a cualquiera.
example.en: Online they call anyone a kuka.

words.note: Short for "Casa Rosada", the pink government house in Plaza de Mayo.

example.es: Hay una marcha frente a la Rosada.
example.en: There's a march in front of the presidential palace.

words.note: The libertarian movement around president Javier Milei, known for "la motosierra" spending cuts.

example.es: El mileísmo ganó fuerza entre los pibes más jóvenes.
example.en: Mileism gained strength among young people.

words.note: Member of Montoneros, the armed Peronist left of the 1970s. Still a charged political word.

example.es: Su tío fue montonero en los años setenta.
example.en: His uncle was a guerrilla in the seventies.

packs.name: Going deeper IV
packs.title: Politics & society · Going deeper IV
packs.about: Parties, protests and the country in the news.

words.note: The mandatory open primary elections, said as one word: "las PASO". Congress suspended them for the 2025 elections.

example.es: En las PASO ganó un candidato que nadie esperaba.
example.en: An unexpected candidate won the primary elections.

words.note: A politician whose image scares off voters for their own party.

example.es: Ese candidato es un piantavotos, nadie lo banca.
example.en: That candidate scares voters away, nobody can stand him.

words.note: Derogatory for someone living on a "plan social", welfare benefits. Politically loaded.

example.es: Mi tío le dice planero a cualquiera que no le cae bien.
example.en: My uncle says anyone he doesn't like lives off welfare.

words.note: A neighborhood political operator who hands out favors and mobilizes voters for a party.

example.es: El puntero del barrio organizó los micros para el acto.
example.en: The local party boss organized the buses for the political event.

words.note: Political wheeling and dealing, deals made behind closed doors. "Rosquear" is the verb; a "rosquero" lives for it.

example.es: Esa ley salió por pura rosca entre los bloques.
example.en: That law passed through secret deals between the parties.

packs.name: Rare gems
packs.title: Politics & society · Rare gems
packs.about: Parties, protests and the country in the news.

words.note: A sudden steep rise in gas, power or transport rates. Always a political fight.

example.es: Con el tarifazo, la cuenta de luz vino el triple.
example.en: With the big price rise, the electricity bill was three times higher.

words.note: Almost always plural, "las tratativas". Common in the news for business or political talks.

example.es: Las tratativas con el sindicato siguen sin acuerdo.
example.en: Negotiations with the union still have no deal.

words.note: Short for "bolchevique". Teasing or dismissive label for a leftist. Sounds dated; today people say "zurdo".

example.es: Le dicen bolche porque siempre anda con la remera del Che.
example.en: They call him a communist because he always wears a Che T-shirt.

words.en: person at rallies for free food
words.note: Mocking term for someone who goes to political rallies for a free choripán. Derogatory.

example.es: Dicen que son choripaneros, pero van por convicción.
example.en: They say they go for the free food, but they go because they believe in it.

words.note: The old compulsory service, ended in 1994. Folk origin: "corre, limpia, barre".

example.es: Mi viejo hizo la colimba en el sur.
example.en: My dad did his military service down south.

packs.name: Essentials
packs.title: Countryside & gauchos · Essentials
packs.about: The pampa, the gaucho and life outside the city.

words.note: A big cattle ranch in the pampas. Many now host tourists for asados and horse rides.

example.es: Hicimos un día de campo en una estancia.
example.en: We spent a day in the country at a ranch.

words.note: The horseman of the pampas. As an adjective it means helpful: "una gauchada" is a favor.

example.es: Mi abuelo era gaucho y domaba caballos.
example.en: My grandfather was a cowboy and tamed horses.

words.note: A farm smaller than an "estancia", often near town. From Quechua.

example.es: Los fines de semana vamos a la chacra de mis tíos.
example.en: On weekends we go to my aunt and uncle's farm.

words.note: Any weed or wild herb. Herbs added to mate are also "yuyos".

example.es: El jardín está lleno de yuyos, hay que cortar el pasto.
example.en: The garden is full of weeds, we need to cut the grass.

words.note: The everyday name for fireflies, seen on summer nights.

example.es: En el campo de mi abuela hay bichitos de luz.
example.en: At my grandma's farm there are fireflies.

packs.name: Going deeper I
packs.title: Countryside & gauchos · Going deeper I
packs.about: The pampa, the gaucho and life outside the city.

words.note: The little bug that rolls into a ball. Every Argentine kid has played with one.

example.es: Los chicos juntaron bichos bolita en el jardín.
example.en: The kids collected pill bugs in the garden.

words.note: Loose pleated pants worn by gauchos and country folk. Not to be confused with panties.

example.es: Para la jineteada se puso bombacha de campo y alpargatas.
example.en: For the rodeo he wore gaucho trousers and canvas shoes.

words.note: Accordion-based folk music and dance from northeastern Argentina.

example.es: En Corrientes todos los fines de semana hay bailes de chamamé.
example.en: In Corrientes there are chamamé dances every weekend.

words.note: A classic game at school fairs and rural festivals.

example.es: En la fiesta del pueblo ganamos la cinchada.
example.en: We won the tug of war at the town festival.

words.note: From an indigenous Patagonian word (Mapuche or Tehuelche). A spell put on someone, usually to make them fall in love.

example.es: Le hicieron un gualicho, está como hipnotizado.
example.en: Someone put a spell on him, he seems hypnotized.

packs.name: Going deeper II
packs.title: Countryside & gauchos · Going deeper II
packs.about: The pampa, the gaucho and life outside the city.

words.note: Gaucho bronco-riding contest, big at country festivals like Jesús María.

example.es: Fuimos a ver la jineteada en el festival de Jesús María.
example.en: We went to watch the rodeo at the Jesús María festival.

words.note: A man from the countryside, the modern gaucho. Also "fellow countryman".

example.es: Un paisano nos indicó el camino al pueblo.
example.en: A countryman showed us the way to town.

words.note: A hired worker on a farm or ranch. "Peón de campo" is the full phrase.

example.es: El peón se levanta a las cinco para ordeñar.
example.en: The farm worker gets up at five to milk the cows.

words.note: Where cows are milked in the countryside. The worker is a "tambero".

example.es: Mi abuelo tenía un tambo cerca de Chivilcoy.
example.en: My grandpa had a dairy farm near Chivilcoy.

words.note: The wooden gate at a ranch entrance or between fields. A symbol of the countryside.

example.es: Cerrá la tranquera así no se escapan las vacas.
example.en: Close the gate so the cows don't get out.

packs.name: Rare gems I
packs.title: Countryside & gauchos · Rare gems I
packs.about: The pampa, the gaucho and life outside the city.

words.note: Traditional folk dance with handkerchiefs, slow and elegant. Not the Brazilian samba.

example.es: En la peña bailaron una zamba con pañuelos.
example.en: At the folk night they danced a zamba with handkerchiefs.

words.note: The Argentine word for skunk; in Spain it's "mofeta". "Olor a zorrino" is a common complaint.

example.es: En la ruta había un zorrino atropellado y el olor era terrible.
example.en: There was a skunk hit by a car on the highway and the smell was awful.

words.note: An untamed horse. Heard only in the countryside and in gaucho books; also said of a rough person.

example.es: Ese caballo es un bagual, nadie lo pudo domar.
example.en: That horse is a wild one, nobody could tame it.

words.note: Old song style from the Andean northwest, sung with a "caja" drum. Not the same as "bagual", a wild horse.

example.es: En Tucumán escuchamos una baguala con caja.
example.en: In Tucumán we heard a traditional folk song with a drum.

packs.name: Rare gems II
packs.title: Countryside & gauchos · Rare gems II
packs.about: The pampa, the gaucho and life outside the city.

words.note: Someone who knows the land perfectly. Also means skilled at anything: "es baqueano".

example.es: Contratamos un baqueano para cruzar la cordillera.
example.en: We hired a local guide to cross the Andes.

words.note: Weighted leather cords thrown to tangle an animal's legs. Indigenous, then gaucho.

example.es: En el museo había boleadoras de piedra.
example.en: At the museum there were old stone throwing weapons.

words.note: Patagonian berry that gives the town El Calafate its name. Legend says eating it brings you back.

example.es: Probé un helado de calafate en el sur.
example.en: I tried Patagonian berry ice cream in the south.

words.note: Dried salted meat, an old gaucho and Andean food.

example.es: En el norte probé una empanada de charqui.
example.en: Up north I tried a dried meat empanada.

words.note: Rural and informal. In the city people say "camioneta".

example.es: Cargamos la leña en la chata y volvimos al campo.
example.en: We loaded the firewood in the pickup and went back to the farm.

packs.name: Rare gems III
packs.title: Countryside & gauchos · Rare gems III
packs.about: The pampa, the gaucho and life outside the city.

words.note: The long knife gauchos carry at the back of the belt, for eating and fighting.

example.es: El gaucho sacó el facón para cortar el asado.
example.en: The gaucho took out his knife to cut the asado.

words.note: Guaraní name everyone uses in the north and many use in Buenos Aires.

example.es: Había un mamboretá verde en la ventana.
example.en: There was a green praying mantis on the window.

words.note: A gaucho on the run from the law, like Martín Fierro. A word from books, not from daily speech.

example.es: Martín Fierro vivió como un matrero.
example.en: Martín Fierro lived as a man on the run.

words.note: Two guitar players improvise rhyming verses in a duel. The singer is a "payador".

example.es: En la fiesta hubo una payada entre dos payadores.
example.en: At the festival two folk singers had a sung poetry contest.

words.note: Gaucho word for a good horse. Used with pride, like "mi pingo".

example.es: Ensilló el pingo y salió al galope.
example.en: He saddled his horse and rode off at a gallop.

packs.name: Rare gems IV
packs.title: Countryside & gauchos · Rare gems IV
packs.about: The pampa, the gaucho and life outside the city.

words.note: The old rural store and bar where gauchos met to drink, play cards and sing.

example.es: Paramos en una pulpería vieja a tomar algo.
example.en: We stopped at an old country store for a drink.

words.note: The short leather whip gauchos use on horseback.

example.es: Colgó el rebenque al lado de la puerta.
example.en: He hung the riding whip next to the door.

words.note: A ruined, abandoned house in the countryside. From Guaraní.

example.es: En el medio del campo quedó una tapera.
example.en: An abandoned house was left in the middle of the field.

words.note: A group of horses following a lead mare. Also used jokingly for a group of people.

example.es: El gaucho arreó la tropilla hasta el corral.
example.en: The gaucho led the group of horses to the corral.

words.note: The day when calves are branded, followed by a big asado.

example.es: Nos invitaron a la yerra de la estancia.
example.en: They invited us to the cattle-marking day at the ranch.

packs.name: Everyday
packs.title: Classic lunfardo · Everyday
packs.about: Tango-era slang that is still understood today.

words.note: Chaos, trouble, a big fuss: "armar quilombo" = to cause a scene. A bit rude: fine with friends, not in formal settings, where "lío" is safe.

example.es: Qué quilombo hay en el centro con la marcha.
example.en: What a mess downtown with the protest march.

words.note: Everyday word for counterfeit, phony or shady: a trucho bill, a trucho doctor, a trucho excuse.

example.es: Me dieron un billete trucho de dos mil en el kiosco.
example.en: They gave me a fake two-thousand bill at the kiosk.

words.note: Angry or in a bad mood: "estar cabrero". A bit old-school; younger people say "caliente" or "re enojado".

example.es: Mi viejo está cabrero porque le choqué el auto.
example.en: My dad is angry because I crashed his car.

words.note: For something old and worn, or a person looking run-down. Informal, heard more from older speakers.

example.es: Tengo un celular cachuzo pero anda bien.
example.en: I have an old, worn-out phone but it works fine.

words.note: Lunfardo for bed. Still used jokingly: "me voy a la catrera" means I am off to bed.

example.es: Estoy muerto, me voy a la catrera.
example.en: I'm very tired, I'm going to bed.

packs.name: Going deeper
packs.title: Classic lunfardo · Going deeper
packs.about: Tango-era slang that is still understood today.

words.note: A small coin; "unas chirolas" means very little money. Mostly older speakers now; "dos mangos" is more usual.

example.es: Me pagan chirolas por este laburo.
example.en: They pay me almost nothing for this job.

words.note: Slang for a pistol, heard in crime news and street talk.

example.es: El tipo sacó un chumbo y todos se tiraron al piso.
example.en: The guy pulled a gun and everyone threw themselves on the floor.

words.note: Lunfardo for ugly or bad. "La cosa se puso fulera" means things turned ugly.

example.es: La cosa se puso fulera y nos fuimos.
example.en: Things got bad and we left.

words.note: Slang for a guitar, especially electric, from rock culture. "Tocar la viola" = to play guitar.

example.es: Trajo la viola y tocamos hasta tarde.
example.en: He brought his guitar and we played until late.

words.note: From Italian "iettatura". A person who brings bad luck is "un yeta"; people also say "mufa": "ese tipo es mufa".

example.es: No lo invites a la cancha, que es yeta.
example.en: Don't invite him to the game, he's bad luck.

packs.name: Rare gems I
packs.title: Classic lunfardo · Rare gems I
packs.about: Tango-era slang that is still understood today.

words.note: Tango-era lunfardo: to abandon someone, especially a lover. Still heard in lyrics and jokes.

example.es: La mina lo amuró y se fue con otro.
example.en: The girl broke up with him and left with another guy.

words.note: Old lunfardo for realizing what is going on. Today people say "avivarse" or "darse cuenta".

example.es: Tardó un montón en apiolarse de que lo estaban cargando.
example.en: It took him a long time to realize they were making fun of him.

words.note: Old lunfardo for sleeping; related to "atorrante" (lazy bum). Older people and jokes; today people say "dormir" or "tirarse un rato".

example.es: Me voy a atorrar un rato después de almorzar.
example.en: I'm going to sleep a bit after lunch.

words.note: Tango-era word for a wealthy, showy man. In Chile and Peru it means "cool" instead.

example.es: Se hace el bacán pero vive con la madre.
example.en: He acts like a rich guy but lives with his mom.

packs.name: Rare gems II
packs.title: Classic lunfardo · Rare gems II
packs.about: Tango-era slang that is still understood today.

words.note: Old lunfardo for a noisy uproar. Heard among older speakers; today people say "quilombo" or "lío".

example.es: Los vecinos armaron un batifondo toda la noche.
example.en: The neighbors made a lot of noise all night.

words.note: Old lunfardo for a beating or a crushing defeat: "dar una biaba". Today people say "paliza".

example.es: Les dieron una biaba: perdieron cinco a cero.
example.en: They got a real beating: they lost five to zero.

words.note: Tango lunfardo for a small room or bachelor pad, often for secret dates.

example.es: Tiene un bulín en San Telmo para las citas.
example.en: He has an apartment in San Telmo for dates.

words.note: Tango-era word for a pimp; also "cafisho", "cafiolo", "fiolo". Now said of a man who lives off others.

example.es: Vive de la novia, es un cafishio.
example.en: He lives off his girlfriend, he's a real freeloader.

words.note: An old, playful, close-embrace style of tango from the early 1900s.

example.es: En la milonga del sábado bailaron canyengue toda la noche.
example.en: At the Saturday milonga they danced canyengue all night.

packs.name: Rare gems III
packs.title: Classic lunfardo · Rare gems III
packs.about: Tango-era slang that is still understood today.

words.note: "Tener carpeta" means having experience with people. Dated; today people say "tener calle". In the news, a "carpetazo" is leaking damaging files on someone.

example.es: Ese vendedor tiene mucha carpeta, te convence de todo.
example.en: That salesman is really experienced, he can sell you anything.

words.note: Old lunfardo from Italian. A soft, almost affectionate insult; today people say "salame" or "tonto".

example.es: No seas chitrulo, así no se hace.
example.en: Don't be an idiot, that's not how you do it.

words.note: The broken Spanish of Italian immigrants around 1900. Now used for any language mash-up.

example.es: Mi abuelo hablaba un cocoliche que nadie entendía.
example.en: My grandpa spoke an Italian-Spanish mix nobody understood.

words.note: A cocky, flashy street guy from old Buenos Aires tango lyrics.

example.es: En el tango, el compadrito siempre anda con cuchillo.
example.en: In tango, the tough guy always carries a knife.

words.note: Old lunfardo from "engrupir", to fool. Someone full of themselves; today people say "agrandado".

example.es: Desde que es gerente anda re engrupido.
example.en: Since he became manager he's really arrogant.

packs.name: Rare gems IV
packs.title: Classic lunfardo · Rare gems IV
packs.about: Tango-era slang that is still understood today.

words.note: Old lunfardo for gambling, especially cards and horses. Today people say "la timba" or "el juego".

example.es: Perdió el sueldo entero en el escolazo.
example.en: He lost his whole paycheck gambling.

words.note: Old lunfardo for running away, like "piantar"; can also mean to steal. Today people say "rajar".

example.es: Cuando vio a la cana, se espiantó.
example.en: When he saw the police, he ran away.

words.note: Lunfardo for false, two-faced or poor quality. Used for people and things. Older spelling: "fayuto".

example.es: No le creas, es un tipo falluto.
example.en: Don't believe him, he is a dishonest guy.

words.note: From French "fané": shabby, past its best. Today it lives only in the tango line "fané y descangayada"; people say "gastado".

example.es: Como dice el tango: "fané y descangayada".
example.en: As the tango says: "worn out and falling apart".

words.note: Old lunfardo for a hat, from Italian "fungo", mushroom. Tango and grandparents.

example.es: Mi abuelo nunca salía sin el funyi.
example.en: My grandpa never went out without his hat.

packs.name: Rare gems V
packs.title: Classic lunfardo · Rare gems V
packs.about: Tango-era slang that is still understood today.

words.note: Old lunfardo for prison, heard in tangos and old crime stories. Today people say "cana": "está en cana".

example.es: Por robar autos terminó en la gayola.
example.en: He ended up in jail for stealing cars.

words.note: Old lunfardo for looking at or sizing something up; also to know. Today people say "mirar" or "fichar".

example.es: Junalo a ese tipo, algo trama.
example.en: Look at that guy, he is planning something.

words.note: Tango-era word for a knife-carrying tough guy from the poor edges of old Buenos Aires.

example.es: En los tangos siempre aparece un malevo con cuchillo.
example.en: In tangos there's always a thug with a knife.

words.note: Lunfardo from Italian "mangiare". Mostly heard as "¿manyás?" (you get it?); can also mean to eat. Today people say "¿entendés?" or "¿cazás?".

example.es: Esto es así y no se discute, ¿manyás?
example.en: That's how it is, no arguing, get it?

packs.name: Rare gems VI
packs.title: Classic lunfardo · Rare gems VI
packs.about: Tango-era slang that is still understood today.

words.note: Jokey word for a dictionary, literally "donkey-killer". Older people and teachers still say it.

example.es: Buscalo en el mataburros si no sabés qué significa.
example.en: Look it up in the dictionary if you don't know what it means.

words.note: Lunfardo for a trick or dirty business, often political. A bit old-fashioned but understood.

example.es: Esa licitación fue una matufia de principio a fin.
example.en: That public contract was a scam from start to finish.

words.note: Old lunfardo for being broke; adjective "mishio". Today people say "estar seco" or "no tener un mango".

example.es: Después de la crisis vino la mishiadura.
example.en: After the crisis came the hard times.

words.note: Tango-era word for a peso or money in general. Still heard jokingly: "unos morlacos".

example.es: Me salió unos cuantos morlacos arreglar el auto.
example.en: Fixing the car cost me a lot of money.

words.note: Tango-era word for an attractive young woman. Only in lyrics today: do not use it as a compliment; say "linda".

example.es: En ese tango le canta a una papusa del barrio.
example.en: In that tango he sings to a pretty girl from the neighborhood.

packs.name: Rare gems VII
packs.title: Classic lunfardo · Rare gems VII
packs.about: Tango-era slang that is still understood today.

words.note: Old lunfardo for a good-for-nothing who avoids work. A little funny; today people say "vago".

example.es: Tiene treinta años y sigue siendo un pelandrún.
example.en: He is thirty and still a lazy guy.

words.note: Classic tango word for a woman or lover. Today heard only in lyrics or as a joke.

example.es: La percanta lo dejó y él escribió un tango.
example.en: His girl left him and he wrote a tango.

words.note: Lunfardo for crazy, famous from the tango "Balada para un loco": "ya sé que estoy piantao".

example.es: Ese tipo está medio piantado, habla solo.
example.en: That guy is a bit crazy, he talks to himself.

words.note: Lunfardo "piantarse": to take off or run away. Heard in tango and with a playful tone.

example.es: Cuando llegó la cana, se piantaron todos.
example.en: When the police came, everyone ran away.

words.note: Old lunfardo for head. Heard jokingly; today people say "cabeza", or "bocho" and "coco" among friends.

example.es: Me pegué en la sabiola con la puerta del auto.
example.en: I hit my head on the car door.

packs.name: Everyday
packs.title: Vesre · Everyday
packs.about: Words said backwards: feca, jermu, toga.

words.en: to pay; to be worth it
words.note: Vesre of "pagar": "¿quién garpa?". Also "garpa" = it is worth it, it is good: "ese bar garpa".

example.es: ¿Quién garpa la cena hoy?
example.en: Who's paying for dinner today?

words.note: From vesre of "batidor", an informer. Today: someone mean, unfriendly or who spoils the fun. Also spelled "ortiba".

example.es: No seas ortiva, dejanos quedarnos un rato más.
example.en: Don't be mean, let us stay a bit longer.

words.note: Vesre of "hotel": rooms rented by the hour for couples. Informal; the sign on the building says "albergue transitorio".

example.es: Como viven con los viejos, van a un telo.
example.en: Since they live with their parents, they go to a love motel.

words.note: "Quilombo" said backwards, a bit softer and playful. A mess, chaos or a problem.

example.es: Qué bolonqui hay en la avenida, no avanza nadie.
example.en: What a mess on the avenue, nobody is moving.

words.note: "Borracho" said backwards. Playful, for someone who is drunk or who drinks a lot.

example.es: Tu amigo está re choborra, pedile un taxi.
example.en: Your friend is really drunk, call him a taxi.

packs.name: Going deeper I
packs.title: Vesre · Going deeper I
packs.about: Words said backwards: feca, jermu, toga.

words.note: Vesre of "café". Playful, heard among friends and in old-school Buenos Aires bars.

example.es: ¿Vamos a tomar un feca a la esquina?
example.en: Shall we grab a coffee at the corner place?

words.note: Vesre of "amigo". Friendly and a bit old-school; also used ironically.

example.es: Este es Juan, un gomía del barrio.
example.en: This is Juan, a buddy from the neighborhood.

words.note: Vesre of "mujer": a wife or girlfriend. Old-school men's talk about their own partner among friends; it can sound disrespectful in polite company.

example.es: Hoy no salgo, me quedo con la jermu.
example.en: I'm not going out tonight, I'm staying in with the wife.

words.note: Vesre of "calor". Jokey way to complain about a hot day.

example.es: Qué lorca que hace hoy, no se puede salir.
example.en: It is so hot today, you cannot go out.

words.note: Vesre of "camión". Playful; everyone understands it, but most people just say "camión".

example.es: Nos quedamos atrás de un mionca en la ruta.
example.en: We got stuck behind a truck on the highway.

packs.name: Going deeper II
packs.title: Vesre · Going deeper II
packs.about: Words said backwards: feca, jermu, toga.

words.note: Vesre of "baño". Playful, heard among friends.

example.es: Esperame un toque que voy al ñoba.
example.en: Wait a sec, I'm going to the bathroom.

words.note: Vesre of "tira", old slang for police. Street slang, a bit rough; not something you'd say to an officer.

example.es: Cuidado, que en la esquina hay un rati.
example.en: Careful, there's a cop on the corner.

words.note: Vesre of "doctor". Friendly; used for doctors and also lawyers. Say it about them, not to them in a formal visit.

example.es: Mañana tengo turno con el tordo.
example.en: Tomorrow I have an appointment with the doctor.

words.note: Vesre of "uruguayo". Friendly teasing between neighbors across the river.

example.es: Mi cuñado es yorugua y toma mate todo el día.
example.en: My brother-in-law is Uruguayan and drinks mate all day.

words.note: Vesre of "pelado", bald. Understood but rarely said; everyone says "pelado".

example.es: El dolape de la barra es el dueño del bar.
example.en: The bald guy at the bar is the owner.

packs.name: Rare gems
packs.title: Vesre · Rare gems
packs.about: Words said backwards: feca, jermu, toga.

words.note: Vesre of "tango". Lives in lyrics, band names and among tango lovers; in normal talk people just say "tango".

example.es: En ese bar de San Telmo pasan puro gotán.
example.en: In that bar in San Telmo they play only tango.

words.note: From vesre of "viejo" plus an ending. Jokey, a bit disrespectful. Female: "jovata".

example.es: El jovato del tercero se queja de todo.
example.en: The old man on the third floor complains about everything.

words.note: Vesre of "calle". "Tener lleca" = to have street smarts, like "tener calle".

example.es: Ese pibe tiene lleca, sabe moverse.
example.en: That kid has street smarts, he knows how to handle himself.

words.note: Vesre-style lunfardo from "pantalón". Often plural: "los lompas". Informal.

example.es: Se me rompió el lompa jugando al fútbol.
example.en: I ripped my pants playing football.

words.note: Vesre of "cabeza". Old lunfardo, heard only in tango or as a joke. Today people say "la cabeza" or "el bocho".

example.es: Usá la zabeca antes de hablar.
example.en: Use your head before you talk.

packs.name: Essentials I
packs.title: Expressions · Essentials I
packs.about: Idioms and set phrases.

words.note: "Estar al pedo": to be idle. "Es al pedo": it's pointless. A bit crude; everyone says it with friends, but not in formal situations.

example.es: Estoy al pedo, ¿querés que te ayude con algo?
example.en: I'm doing nothing, want me to help with something?

words.note: To notice or care about someone. "No me da bola" = he ignores me. Used by everyone.

example.es: Le escribo todos los días y no me da bola.
example.en: I text him every day and he ignores me.

words.note: "Estar en pedo" means to be drunk, or to talk nonsense. Very common.

example.es: Anoche volvió re en pedo del cumple.
example.en: Last night he came back very drunk from the party.

words.note: For sympathy ("that's a lot to deal with") or to say someone is being extra.

example.es: Mudarte y cambiar de trabajo juntos es un montón.
example.en: Moving and changing jobs at once is a lot.

words.note: Rude, unpleasant or negative. "No seas mala onda" = don't be mean. Very common.

example.es: No seas mala onda y prestame el cargador.
example.en: Don't be mean and lend me the charger.

packs.name: Essentials II
packs.title: Expressions · Essentials II
packs.about: Idioms and set phrases.

words.note: Literally "not even drunk". Very common and casual, a bit crude.

example.es: ¿Ir a trabajar un domingo? Ni en pedo.
example.en: Go to work on a Sunday? Absolutely no way.

words.note: A reaction to surprising news, good or bad. The "te" is fixed; you are not doubting the person.

example.es: ¿Renunció? ¡No te puedo creer!
example.en: She quit? I can't believe it!

words.note: The normal way to say just in case, much more common than "por si acaso".

example.es: Llevá paraguas por las dudas.
example.en: Take an umbrella just in case.

words.note: At max volume, speed or effort: "la música al mango". "Estoy al mango" = very busy or very excited.

example.es: Los vecinos tienen la música al mango otra vez.
example.en: The neighbors have the music very loud again.

words.note: Literally to shit yourself laughing. Very common and only mildly rude.

example.es: Nos cagamos de risa con el video.
example.en: We laughed so hard at the video.

packs.name: Essentials III
packs.title: Expressions · Essentials III
packs.about: Idioms and set phrases.

words.note: "Me da bronca" = it annoys me. "Bronca" is anger; very Argentine and everyday.

example.es: Me da bronca que siempre llegue tarde.
example.en: It makes me mad that he's always late.

words.note: Done kindly, for free. "Te lo digo de onda" means I say it in good faith.

example.es: Me arregló la compu de onda, no me cobró nada.
example.en: He fixed my computer as a favor, didn't charge me.

words.note: In big trouble, with no easy way out. Also "estar en el horno". Very common and informal.

example.es: Si mañana no entrego el informe, estoy al horno.
example.en: If I don't hand in the report tomorrow, I'm in trouble.

words.note: To pretend you don't know or didn't notice. Rude but very common.

example.es: No te hagas el boludo, sabés de qué hablo.
example.en: Don't pretend you don't know, you know what I'm talking about.

words.note: "¡Qué mala leche!" = what bad luck. "Tener mala leche" = to be unlucky. "De mala leche" = with bad intentions.

example.es: Lo hizo de mala leche, no fue sin querer.
example.en: He did it with bad intentions, it wasn't an accident.

packs.name: Essentials IV
packs.title: Expressions · Essentials IV
packs.about: Idioms and set phrases.

words.note: "Cargar" means to tease. "¿Me estás cargando?" = are you joking with me? Very common.

example.es: ¿Aprobaste sin estudiar? ¿Me estás cargando?
example.en: You passed without studying? Are you kidding me?

words.note: Strong refusal, a clean alternative to "ni en pedo". Informal.

example.es: ¿Prestarle plata otra vez? Ni a palos.
example.en: Lend him money again? No way.

words.note: Reassuring phrase: no big deal. Very common in everyday talk.

example.es: No te hagas problema, yo pago esta vez.
example.en: Don't worry about it, I'll pay this time.

words.note: Literally put your batteries in: get moving, focus. Said by parents, bosses, friends.

example.es: Ponete las pilas, que el examen es el lunes.
example.en: Try harder, the exam is Monday.

words.en: to look good; to look like
words.note: "Tiene pinta" or "tiene buena pinta" = it looks good. "Tiene pinta de..." = it looks like: "tiene pinta de caro".

example.es: Este restaurante tiene pinta, entremos.
example.en: This restaurant looks good, let's go in.

packs.name: Essentials V
packs.title: Expressions · Essentials V
packs.about: Idioms and set phrases.

words.note: Literally to shift down a gear. Said to someone who is too angry, too stressed or working too much.

example.es: Bajá un cambio, no es para tanto.
example.en: Calm down, it's not such a big deal.

words.note: Like a token dropping in an old payphone. "Me cayó la ficha" = I finally understood.

example.es: Recién hoy me cayó la ficha de que me mudo.
example.en: I only realized today that I'm moving.

words.note: To get someone worked up or keep pushing them to do something. "Estar manija" = to be very excited and impatient.

example.es: No le des manija, que después se pelea.
example.en: Don't get him worked up, he'll end up fighting.

words.note: To have too much work or too many problems. Can also mean very much in love. Informal.

example.es: No puedo hablar ahora, estoy hasta las manos.
example.en: I can't talk now, I'm very busy.

words.note: To keep someone company or support them. "Haceme la gamba" = come with me, be there.

example.es: Haceme la gamba y acompañame al médico.
example.en: Do me a favor and come with me to the doctor.

packs.name: Essentials VI
packs.title: Expressions · Essentials VI
packs.about: Idioms and set phrases.

words.note: To try to be clever at others' expense or cut corners. "No te hagas el vivo".

example.es: No te hagas el vivo y hacé la fila como todos.
example.en: Don't try to be clever and wait in line like everyone.

words.note: To build a story in your head, often jealousy or false hopes. "No te hagas la película".

example.es: Me saludó y ya me hice la película de que le gusto.
example.en: He said hi and I already imagined he likes me.

words.note: To bring energy and a good attitude to something. "Ponele onda" is said to someone who is being negative or lazy.

example.es: Dale, ponele onda, que es tu cumpleaños.
example.en: Come on, make an effort, it's your birthday.

words.note: "La rompiste": you did great. Said of a player, a band, or a friend after an exam. Mostly used in the past.

example.es: La rompiste en la entrevista, seguro te llaman.
example.en: You did great in the interview, they'll call you for sure.

words.note: To talk without knowing, inventing answers as you go. Also "mandar fruta".

example.es: No estudió nada y tiró fruta en todo el examen.
example.en: He didn't study at all and made things up in the whole exam.

packs.name: Essentials VII
packs.title: Expressions · Essentials VII
packs.about: Idioms and set phrases.

words.note: Literally at the farts. For doing something very quickly.

example.es: Salí a los pedos porque llegaba tarde.
example.en: I left in a big rush because I was late.

words.note: The Argentine coin toss. "Ceca" is tails; Spain says "cara o cruz".

example.es: Tiramos una moneda: cara o ceca, ¿qué elegís?
example.en: Let's flip a coin: heads or tails, which do you pick?

words.note: All at once, without stopping.

example.es: Se tomó la cerveza de un saque.
example.en: He drank the beer in one go.

words.note: To expose or tell on someone, or put them on the spot. Informal.

example.es: Mi hermano me mandó al frente con mamá.
example.en: My brother told on me to mom.

words.note: To take the bait of a trick or provocation. "No pises el palito" = don't fall for it.

example.es: Le dije que era feriado y pisó el palito.
example.en: I told him it was a holiday and he believed it.

packs.name: Everyday
packs.title: Expressions · Everyday
packs.about: Idioms and set phrases.

words.note: "Se pudrió todo": a fight or chaos started. "Se re pudrió" is stronger.

example.es: Llegó el ex de ella a la fiesta y se pudrió todo.
example.en: Her ex came to the party and things got ugly.

words.note: Literally "if I tell you, I'd be lying". A friendly way to admit you're not sure.

example.es: ¿A qué hora cierra? Si te digo te miento.
example.en: What time does it close? I honestly couldn't tell you.

words.note: At full speed, flying. Informal, common among younger speakers.

example.es: Salí a las chapas porque perdía el tren.
example.en: I left very fast because I was going to miss the train.

words.note: Doing something clumsily, lurching from one problem to the next. Often said about the economy.

example.es: El país sigue a los tumbos, como siempre.
example.en: The country keeps having problems, as always.

words.note: Pointlessly, in vain. Polite cousin of "al pedo". Colloquial.

example.es: Fui hasta el banco al divino botón, estaba cerrado.
example.en: I went all the way to the bank for nothing, it was closed.

packs.name: Going deeper I
packs.title: Expressions · Going deeper I
packs.about: Idioms and set phrases.

words.note: A "poroto" is a bean, once used to keep score in card games. To earn credit for something.

example.es: Con ese asado te anotaste un poroto con mis viejos.
example.en: With that barbecue you scored a point with my parents.

words.note: Literally "tied with wire": fixed in a quick, cheap way that may fail at any moment. Said of things, plans and the country.

example.es: El sistema de la oficina está todo atado con alambre.
example.en: The office system is barely holding together.

words.note: To lecture or tell people what to think, often politically. "Bajada de línea": preachy message.

example.es: La peli está buena pero baja línea todo el tiempo.
example.en: The movie is good but it keeps pushing its ideas.

words.note: Sarcastic reply to something obvious. Playful, used by all ages.

example.es: ¿Que hace calor en enero? Chocolate por la noticia.
example.en: It's hot in January? Obviously.

words.note: To turn someone down coldly, often someone who is flirting with you. "Me cortó el rostro". Informal.

example.es: La invité a bailar y me cortó el rostro.
example.en: I asked her to dance and she said no.

packs.name: Going deeper II
packs.title: Expressions · Going deeper II
packs.about: Idioms and set phrases.

words.en: to cross to Uruguay or Europe
words.note: "El charco" is the River Plate, or the Atlantic when going to Europe.

example.es: Este finde cruzamos el charco a Montevideo.
example.en: This weekend we're crossing the river to Montevideo.

words.note: To beat badly, or to scold hard.

example.es: River le dio un pesto a Boca: cuatro a cero.
example.en: River beat Boca badly: four to zero.

words.note: A curious detail. Heard a lot on TV and radio.

example.es: Dato de color: el dueño del bar es primo de Messi.
example.en: Fun fact: the bar's owner is Messi's cousin.

words.note: Boxing image: knocked down on the canvas. Also means exhausted or down. Informal.

example.es: Este mes estoy en la lona, no puedo salir.
example.en: I have no money this month, I can't go out.

words.note: Said of someone naive or inexperienced: "le falta calle".

example.es: A ese pibe le falta calle, se cree todo.
example.en: That kid has no life experience, he believes everything.

packs.name: Going deeper III
packs.title: Expressions · Going deeper III
packs.about: Idioms and set phrases.

words.note: To cut someone off for good after they let you down.

example.es: Desde esa pelea le hizo la cruz y no le habla.
example.en: Since that fight she is done with him and doesn't talk to him.

words.note: To pretend you didn't hear or notice, to avoid something. "Sota" is the jack in Spanish cards. The everyday (crude) version is "hacerse el boludo".

example.es: Le pedí la plata que me debe y se hizo el sota.
example.en: I asked for the money he owes me and he pretended not to understand.

words.note: To skip school without your parents knowing. Also "ratearse".

example.es: Ayer me hice la rata y fui a la plaza.
example.en: Yesterday I skipped school and went to the park.

words.note: To fret or get upset over something. "No te hagas mala sangre" = don't let it get to you.

example.es: No te hagas mala sangre por eso, no vale la pena.
example.en: Don't get upset about it, it's not worth it.

words.note: Cut the small talk: "vamos a los bifes". "Bife" is steak. Informal.

example.es: Bueno, dejémonos de vueltas y vamos a los bifes.
example.en: OK, enough talking around it, let's get to the point.

packs.name: Going deeper IV
packs.title: Expressions · Going deeper IV
packs.about: Idioms and set phrases.

words.note: To lose control or go too far, in behavior or prices. "Se fue al pasto" is very common.

example.es: Con los precios del restaurante se fueron al pasto.
example.en: The restaurant went too far with the prices.

words.note: To brag or pretend you're more than you are. Informal, slightly critical.

example.es: Se manda la parte con el auto, pero es del padre.
example.en: He shows off with the car, but it's his dad's.

words.note: To sow discord with gossip or comments. "Púa" is a spike. Informal.

example.es: No le hagas caso, siempre está metiendo púa.
example.en: Ignore him, he's always causing trouble.

words.note: Said of a very kind, good-hearted person: "es un pan de Dios".

example.es: Tu abuelo es un pan de Dios, ayuda a todo el mundo.
example.en: Your grandpa is a very kind person, he helps everyone.

words.note: To play or work with guts and heart. Big in football talk. "Hay que ponerle garra".

example.es: Perdimos, pero el equipo le puso garra.
example.en: We lost, but the team tried very hard.

packs.name: Going deeper V
packs.title: Expressions · Going deeper V
packs.about: Idioms and set phrases.

words.note: To be firm with someone who is going too far. Colloquial.

example.es: Si sigue llegando tarde, le voy a poner los puntos.
example.en: If he keeps coming late, I'll have a serious talk with him.

words.note: Literally "the little lightbulb turns on": you suddenly get an idea.

example.es: De repente se me prendió la lamparita y lo resolví.
example.en: Suddenly I had a bright idea and solved it.

words.note: To be left waiting with no answer, or embarrassed in front of others. "Me dejaste pagando" = you left me with no answer. Informal.

example.es: Saludé a alguien que no me conocía y quedé pagando.
example.en: I waved at someone who didn't know me and ended up looking silly.

words.note: Literally to row it: to keep working hard when things are difficult, especially with money. Often with "hay que".

example.es: Con esta inflación hay que remarla todos los meses.
example.en: With this inflation you have to keep struggling every month.

words.es: salir con los tapones de punta
words.note: Football image: studs up. To react aggressively from the start. Informal.

example.es: Le pregunté algo y salió con los tapones de punta.
example.en: I asked him something and he reacted very angrily.

words.gap: salió con los tapones de punta

packs.name: Going deeper VI
packs.title: Expressions · Going deeper VI
packs.about: Idioms and set phrases.

words.note: Having no skill, especially at football. "Es de madera jugando". Joking tone.

example.es: No lo pongas de arquero, es de madera.
example.en: Don't put him in goal, he's really bad.

words.note: Immediately, right then. "Pucho" is a cigarette butt.

example.es: Lo decidimos sobre el pucho y salió bárbaro.
example.en: We decided it on the spot and it went great.

words.note: Having know-how and street smarts in something. "Tiene mucha cancha con los clientes".

example.es: Dejala hablar a ella, que tiene cancha con esto.
example.en: Let her talk, she has experience with this.

words.note: To have a sure income without effort, often inherited. Colloquial, slightly envious.

example.es: Con la herencia del abuelo tiene la vaca atada.
example.en: With grandpa's inheritance he is rich for life.

words.note: To spend wildly. From rich 1920s Argentines in Paris said to fling butter at restaurant ceilings.

example.es: Ganó la lotería y ahora tira manteca al techo.
example.en: He won the lottery and now he spends money freely.

packs.name: Rare gems I
packs.title: Expressions · Rare gems I
packs.about: Idioms and set phrases.

words.note: To treat something as a joke: "se toma todo para la joda". "Tomar a alguien para la joda" = to make fun of them. Informal.

example.es: Te hablo en serio, no te lo tomes para la joda.
example.en: I'm serious, don't treat it as a joke.

words.note: Means it is too late and nobody will listen to your complaint. Gardel was the great tango singer. Old-school; today people just say "arreglate".

example.es: Si perdés el ticket, después andá a cantarle a Gardel.
example.en: If you lose the receipt, complaining won't help later.

words.note: To kiss and touch each other for a long time. Not crude, but dated; today people say "chapar" or "transar".

example.es: Estaban franeleando en el sillón toda la noche.
example.en: They were kissing and touching on the couch all night.

words.note: To chat about nothing in particular.

example.es: Nos quedamos hasta tarde hablando de bueyes perdidos.
example.en: We stayed up late talking about nothing important.

words.note: To hold your ground and not back down. Old gaucho expression; today people say "plantarse" or "no aflojar".

example.es: Hay que hacer pata ancha y no aflojar.
example.en: We have to stand firm and not give in.

packs.name: Rare gems II
packs.title: Expressions · Rare gems II
packs.about: Idioms and set phrases.

words.note: To skip school. Said in Córdoba, Rosario and San Juan; in Buenos Aires people say "hacerse la rata" or "ratearse".

example.es: En la secundaria nos hacíamos la chupina los viernes.
example.en: In high school we skipped class on Fridays.

words.note: Playful twist on ipso facto, with pucho (cigarette butt).

example.es: Lo llamé y vino ipso pucho.
example.en: I called him and he came right away.

words.es: más perdido que turco en la neblina
words.note: Joking way to say totally lost. "Turco" is the old nickname for Syrian and Lebanese immigrants, so it can sound a little offensive. Today people say "re perdido".

example.es: Llegué a la reunión más perdido que turco en la neblina.
example.en: I got to the meeting completely lost.

words.gap: más perdido que turco en la neblina

words.note: To cheat or pass off something bad as good. Colloquial.

example.es: El mecánico nos metió la mula con los repuestos.
example.en: The mechanic cheated us with the parts.

words.note: To flirt with someone. "Galgos" are greyhounds. Old-school; today people say "tirar onda" or "tirar los perros".

example.es: Toda la noche le estuvo tirando los galgos a tu prima.
example.en: He was flirting with your cousin all night.

packs.name: Essentials I
packs.title: Puteadas · Essentials I
packs.about: Insults, swearing and rude words. Adults only.

words.note: "Me cagaron" means I got ripped off or betrayed. Also "cagar a alguien": to cheat on them.

example.es: En ese taller te cagan con los precios.
example.en: That garage cheats you on prices.

words.note: All-purpose curse. "Me importa un carajo" is I don't give a damn; "al carajo" is to hell.

example.es: ¡Carajo, me olvidé las llaves!
example.en: Damn, I forgot my keys!

words.note: Besides ass, it means luck: "qué culo" means how lucky. "Tener culo" is to be lucky.

example.es: ¡Qué culo, ganó la rifa dos veces!
example.en: What luck, she won the raffle twice!

words.note: Goes after any noun to trash it. Very common.

example.es: Este celular de mierda se apaga solo.
example.en: This shitty phone keeps turning itself off.

words.note: Insult for someone mean or disloyal. Literally a condom. Very common among friends too.

example.es: No seas forro, devolvele la plata.
example.en: Don't be a jerk, give him back the money.

packs.name: Essentials II
packs.title: Puteadas · Essentials II
packs.about: Insults, swearing and rude words. Adults only.

words.note: Strong insult. Also said with admiration: "qué hijo de puta, cómo juega".

example.es: Ese hijo de puta me robó la bici.
example.en: That son of a bitch stole my bike.

words.note: Classic exclamation of anger or surprise.

example.es: ¡La puta madre, me olvidé las llaves!
example.en: Fuck, I forgot my keys!

words.note: One of the most common Argentine insults, stronger than "boludo". Crude.

example.es: El pelotudo ese se me cruzó en rojo.
example.en: That idiot ran the red light right in front of me.

words.note: Vulgar exclamation of surprise or anger. Also "mandar a la mierda": to tell someone to go to hell.

example.es: ¡A la mierda, mirá lo que sale este café!
example.en: Holy shit, look what this coffee costs!

words.note: Very common rude way to say no or tell someone to go away. Can be playful among friends.

example.es: ¿Que yo pague todo? Andá a cagar.
example.en: Me pay for everything? Go to hell.

packs.name: Essentials III
packs.title: Puteadas · Essentials III
packs.about: Insults, swearing and rude words. Adults only.

words.note: Crude but very common: to scold someone hard.

example.es: Mi vieja me cagó a pedos por llegar tarde.
example.en: My mom yelled at me for coming home late.

words.note: In Argentina it only means to have sex. Never use it for "to take", say "agarrar".

example.es: Esos dos cogen como conejos.
example.en: Those two fuck like rabbits.

words.note: Literally in balls. "Estar en bolas" is to be naked, or to have no idea about a topic.

example.es: Fui al examen en bolas, no estudié nada.
example.en: I went to the exam unprepared, I didn't study at all.

words.note: Strong curse of anger or frustration. Literally the parrot's pussy.

example.es: ¡La concha de la lora, se me cortó la luz!
example.en: Fucking hell, the power went out!

words.note: One of the strongest insults. Also shouted at referees and at the TV.

example.es: ¡La concha de tu madre, me chocaste el auto!
example.en: You motherfucker, you hit my car!

packs.name: Essentials IV
packs.title: Puteadas · Essentials IV
packs.about: Insults, swearing and rude words. Adults only.

words.note: Strong insult. "La puta que lo parió" is also said about things, even in joy.

example.es: ¡La puta que te parió, me asustaste!
example.en: Son of a bitch, you scared me!

words.note: Crude word for ass. "¡Qué orto!" = what luck; "de orto" = by pure luck. "Como el orto" = really badly: "me fue como el orto".

example.es: Aprobé sin estudiar, ¡qué orto que tuve!
example.en: I passed without studying, what luck I had!

words.note: Something stupid or pointless. Crude but constant in casual talk.

example.es: No digas pelotudeces, sabés que te quiero.
example.en: Don't say stupid things, you know I love you.

words.note: To insult someone with swear words, or just to swear in anger. Informal and a bit rude, but very common.

example.es: El colectivero me puteó porque crucé mal.
example.en: The bus driver swore at me because I crossed badly.

words.note: Vulgar but extremely common. "No me rompas las pelotas" means stop bothering me. An annoying person is a "rompepelotas".

example.es: Dejá de romper las pelotas, que estoy laburando.
example.en: Stop annoying me, I'm working.

packs.name: Essentials V
packs.title: Puteadas · Essentials V
packs.about: Insults, swearing and rude words. Adults only.

words.note: A big scare. "Me pegué un cagazo" = I got very scared.

example.es: Me pegué un cagazo cuando sonó la alarma.
example.en: I got really scared when the alarm went off.

words.note: From "cagarse", to get scared. Common taunt among friends.

example.es: Dale, tirate a la pileta, no seas cagón.
example.en: Come on, jump in the pool, don't be chicken.

words.note: Vulgar for something cheap or bad quality.

example.es: Este cargador choto no anda más.
example.en: This crappy charger doesn't work anymore.

words.note: "Me chupa un huevo" means I couldn't care less. Literally to suck a ball.

example.es: Lo que diga tu primo me chupa un huevo.
example.en: I don't care at all what your cousin says.

words.note: Very vulgar. Base of the classic curse "la concha de tu madre". Avoid it for seashell.

example.es: ¡La concha de tu hermana, perdí el tren!
example.en: Fuck, I missed the train!

packs.name: Essentials VI
packs.title: Puteadas · Essentials VI
packs.about: Insults, swearing and rude words. Adults only.

words.note: For something very expensive or very hard. "Un huevo" alone means a lot.

example.es: Esas zapatillas me costaron un huevo.
example.en: Those sneakers cost me a fortune.

words.note: From "cagador" in vesre: someone who cheats people. Also said of rich people who exploit others.

example.es: Ese tipo es un garca, no le prestes plata.
example.en: That guy is dishonest, don't lend him money.

words.note: Vulgar word for penis. "Una garcha" means something is crap.

example.es: Esta película es una garcha.
example.en: This movie is crap.

words.note: Very vulgar word for having sex.

example.es: Dice que anoche garchó con su ex.
example.en: He says he fucked his ex last night.

words.note: Literally an orphan. Used as an insult, or affectionately among friends and for kids.

example.es: Qué guacho, se comió todas las empanadas.
example.en: What a bastard, he ate all the empanadas.

packs.name: Essentials VII
packs.title: Puteadas · Essentials VII
packs.about: Insults, swearing and rude words. Adults only.

words.note: To make a big mistake. "Una cagada" alone means a screw-up or a crappy thing.

example.es: Me mandé una cagada y borré todo el trabajo.
example.en: I messed up and deleted all my work.

words.note: Literally someone who masturbates a lot. Also used for a lazy person.

example.es: No seas pajero y ayudame con la mudanza.
example.en: Don't be a lazy jerk and help me with the move.

words.note: Very vulgar word for penis. Very common in "me chupa la pija" = I don't give a fuck.

example.es: Me chupa la pija lo que piensen.
example.en: I don't give a fuck what they think.

words.note: An annoying person. Also "rompepelotas" and "hinchapelotas". See "romper las pelotas".

example.es: Mi vecino es un rompebolas, se queja por todo.
example.en: My neighbor is a pain in the ass, he complains about everything.

words.note: Vulgar. Literally a turd; mostly used as an insult for a mean or dishonest person.

example.es: Ese tipo es un sorete, no le prestes más plata.
example.en: That guy is a piece of shit, don't lend him money anymore.

packs.name: Essentials VIII
packs.title: Puteadas · Essentials VIII
packs.about: Insults, swearing and rude words. Adults only.

words.note: Crude: to beat someone up with punches. "Piña" is a punch.

example.es: Si lo encuentro, lo cago a piñas.
example.en: If I find him, I'll beat him up.

words.note: Very rude way to tell someone to shut up. "Orto" means ass.

example.es: Cerrá el orto un rato, que no escucho la tele.
example.en: Shut the fuck up for a sec, I can't hear the TV.

words.note: Vulgar. "Me importa una chota" means I don't give a damn.

example.es: Me importa una chota lo que digan.
example.en: I don't give a damn what they say.

words.note: Street insult for someone who obeys and serves others, a nobody. Said about a woman it means prostitute or escort today, so never call a woman "gato".

example.es: No seas gato, no le hagas la tarea.
example.en: Don't be his servant, don't do his homework for him.

words.note: "Estoy hasta las pelotas" means I have way too much to do. "Hasta las pelotas de algo" can also mean fed up with it.

example.es: Esta semana estoy hasta las pelotas de laburo.
example.en: This week I am very busy with work.

packs.name: Everyday
packs.title: Puteadas · Everyday
packs.about: Insults, swearing and rude words. Adults only.

example.es: Me rompí el orto estudiando e igual me bocharon.
example.en: I studied really hard and they still failed me.

words.note: Literally to have your balls full. Also "estar con las pelotas llenas".

example.es: Tengo las pelotas llenas de este tráfico.
example.en: I am so fed up with this traffic.

words.note: Vulgar when it means aroused. "Alzado/a" can also mean arrogant or rebellious.

example.es: Anda re alzado desde que volvió de vacaciones.
example.en: He's been so horny since he got back from vacation.

words.note: Rude way to call someone ugly, almost always said about women; sexist and hurtful. Understand it, do not use it. Originally a bundle of smuggled goods.

example.es: Qué forro, le dijo bagayo a la chica.
example.en: What a jerk, he called the girl ugly.

words.note: Crude way to say someone died, or something broke for good.

example.es: La heladera cagó fuego en pleno verano.
example.en: The fridge died in the middle of summer.

packs.name: Going deeper I
packs.title: Puteadas · Going deeper I
packs.about: Insults, swearing and rude words. Adults only.

words.note: Vulgar word for the vagina. Note: in Mexico "cajeta" is a caramel sauce.

example.es: No digas cajeta delante de tu abuela.
example.en: Don't say pussy in front of your grandma.

words.note: A bit crude. "Tener cara de culo" = to look angry or in a bad mood.

example.es: Vino a la reunión con una cara de culo terrible.
example.en: He came to the meeting with a really angry face.

words.note: Very offensive, with a homophobic tone. Sometimes said of someone who flatters the boss; the normal word for that is "chupamedias". Do not use it.

example.es: Ese chupapija le lleva el café al jefe todos los días.
example.en: That cocksucker brings the boss coffee every day.

words.note: Strong insult for a mean, spiteful person. Female: "conchuda", very harsh. Crude; understand it, do not say it to anyone.

example.es: El conchudo se fue y nos dejó todo el laburo.
example.en: The bastard left and dumped all the work on us.

words.note: A man whose partner cheats on him. Common insult, often shouted at referees.

example.es: Todos sabían menos él, pobre cornudo.
example.en: Everyone except him knew she was cheating on him, poor guy.

example.es: Se enculó porque no lo invitamos al asado.
example.en: He got angry because we didn't invite him to the barbecue.

example.en: Stop jerking off and start studying.

example.en: That actress, I'd totally sleep with her.

words.note: To waste time doing nothing useful, or to act like an idiot. Crude.

example.en: Stop messing around and get to work.
